passage:
People ask me when I knew it was over, and the honest answer is: long before I said so. I'm Rekha. For five months my line was "one more month." Sales were flat, the app's monthly users kept shrinking, and I kept telling the team the next release would fix it.

What I was really protecting was my pride. Two years of my life, my parents' savings. Quitting felt like admitting it had all been wasted.

Then Charu, who ran the accelerator where we'd started, asked to see the numbers. She didn't argue. She just asked, "What would have to be true in three months for you to keep going?" I couldn't answer.

So we wrote it down: kill criteria, with a date. When the date passed and the numbers hadn't moved, I shut it down on purpose. It hurt. But I chose the ending, and that mattered.

qa.q: What was Rekha's line for five months?
qa.a: Rekha's line for five months was "one more month."

qa.q: What was Rekha afraid of underneath the words 'one more month'?
qa.a: Rekha was protecting pride and feared admitting that two years of effort and the parents' savings had been wasted.

qa.q: How did Charu's question help Rekha see the situation more clearly?
qa.a: Asking what would have to be true in three months made Rekha realise there was no answer, and led to written kill criteria with a date.

qa.q: How might Charu have seen the situation from outside?
qa.a: Charu probably saw a founder drifting on hope, and chose to ask a calm question instead of arguing so Rekha could reach the decision independently.

grounding: Rekha keeps saying one more month while evidence says otherwise; an outsider reviews the numbers and kill criteria let Rekha choose an ending.

passage:
Dear Bhavna,
You mentored me at the incubator two years ago, so I hope it's okay to ask for help.
The handloom marketplace is still running. I've said "one more month" to myself since January. It's now August. Orders are down again, and I've put in the last of my own savings. Every time I think of stopping, I think of everything I've already put in, and I can't.
I think that's pride talking. And fear, honestly, of telling everyone I quit.
So I want to do this properly. Could you look at the numbers with me next week, as someone who isn't inside my head? Before we meet I'll write down, in advance, what has to be true by 31 October for me to continue: a number of repeat buyers, and monthly costs covered. If we don't hit it, I'll close it cleanly, with notice to our weavers.
I'd rather choose an ending than drift into one.
Gurpreet

qa.q: Since when has Gurpreet been saying "one more month"?
What feelings does Gurpreet admit are behind the delay?
qa.a: Gurpreet admits pride and fear, especially fear of telling everyone about quitting after putting in so much.

qa.q: What steps does Gurpreet plan to stop drifting?
qa.a: Setting kill criteria in advance for 31 October, asking Bhavna as an outsider to review the numbers, and closing cleanly with notice to the weavers if needed.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see this letter?
qa.a: Bhavna may feel touched to be trusted and relieved that Gurpreet is ready to face the numbers honestly.

grounding: The protagonist keeps saying one more month; seeing pride and fear behind it, they set kill criteria in advance and ask a trusted outsider to review the numbers.

passage: "I kept the cloud-kitchen going for eleven months longer than I should have. I'm Afreen, by the way. Every month I told my friend Tanuja, 'Next month the orders will pick up.' They didn't. I'd put everything into it, and quitting felt like admitting I'd wasted two years. So I kept telling myself stories. Then one night Tanuja, who's an accountant, just asked, 'What number would make you stop?' I didn't have one. That shocked me. So we sat on her floor and wrote them down: if orders stay below a certain level for three months, or if I have to borrow again, I close. We picked a date. Tanuja checked the numbers with me every month, because I couldn't trust myself to. In March, we hit the stop line. I closed it on my own terms, paid everyone, and cried for a week. But I chose it. That mattered."

qa.q: What question did Tanuja ask Afreen?
What was Afreen feeling during those eleven months?
qa.a: Afreen felt afraid and proud, unwilling to admit two years might have been wasted, so kept telling hopeful stories.

qa.q: What helped Afreen choose an ending instead of drifting?
qa.a: Writing down stop criteria and a date in advance, and having Tanuja check the numbers every month as a trusted outsider.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt watching Afreen's stories each month?
qa.a: Tanuja was probably worried and frustrated, but patient enough to ask a clear question and help check the numbers.

grounding: The protagonist kept a failing venture going out of pride and fear; a trusted outsider helped set stop criteria so the ending was chosen, not drifted into.
